name: Bill Hagerty
bio: Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Tennessee Commissioner of Economic and Community Development. Trump-endorsed; $5.3M cash on hand.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No new early childhood education or childcare statements from Hagerty were found in the July 14-20, 2026 window.
early_childhood_ed.details: Senator Hagerty's public appearances during this window (a July 14 Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria' interview on the CLARITY Act, SAVE America Act, and Reconciliation 3.0, plus tributes to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham) did not address early childhood education or childcare. Hagerty declined USA TODAY Network-Tennessee's request for a Senate voter guide interview, which is where his Democratic opponents addressed cost-of-living issues. As backdrop, Tennessee's new Child Care Red Tape Reduction Act took effect this period, streamlining permitting and licensing for early learning facilities; advocates note it does not address the underlying cost of care, which in Tennessee now exceeds the cost of a public university education. More than 300,000 Tennessee children under age 5 need child care, and Nashville-area providers meet only about 56% of that need, according to the Nashville Early Education Coalition. No new early childhood education/childcare statements were found in the July 14-20, 2026 window.

child_hunger.summary: No new SNAP or child hunger statements from Hagerty were found in the July 14-20, 2026 window.
child_hunger.details: Hagerty made no public statements on SNAP, child hunger, or school meals during this period; his tracked media appearance focused on digital-asset legislation, the SAVE America Act, and national defense policy. He declined the USA TODAY Network-Tennessee Senate voter guide interview where affordability topics were raised by his Democratic opponents. As policy backdrop, this week marked roughly one year since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) reshaped SNAP nationally; Tennessee reporting (Civil Eats, July 16) profiled a Tennessee SNAP recipient who lost benefits under OBBBA's expanded work requirements (age exemption raised from 54 to 64), and regional food banks project about 50,000 area households losing an average of $187/month in benefits as the law phases in. Nationally, ProPublica/CBPP data cited this week found at least 776,000 children have lost SNAP benefits since the law's passage, with roughly 1 million fewer children on SNAP nationally as of the most recent data. Tennessee was also slated to begin its SNAP soda/candy purchase restrictions July 31, though a federal court ruling this week cast doubt on USDA's authority to approve such state waivers. No new SNAP/child hunger statements were found from Hagerty in the July 14-20, 2026 window.

parental_support.summary: No new statements on paid leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare costs from Hagerty were found in the July 14-20, 2026 window.
parental_support.details: Hagerty's tracked public communications this week centered on the CLARITY Act, SAVE America Act, Reconciliation 3.0, and remembrances of Sen. Lindsey Graham -- none touching paid leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare affordability. He was unavailable for the USA TODAY Network-Tennessee Senate voter guide interview, in which his Democratic rivals discussed affordability pressures on Tennessee families. As context, a new SmartAsset study released this week found Memphis and Nashville rank among the most affordable major U.S. metros for raising a child in 2026 (about $19,922 and $21,216 per year respectively), yet child care alone still consumes roughly 17-20% of the average Tennessee family's income, with average child care costs around $14,000 per child annually -- more than in-state college tuition. No new parental-support statements were found from Hagerty in the July 14-20, 2026 window.
